coding_context.description: Compared to working together with a moderately superior partner who provides encouraging statements that use the exclusive “you” pronoun, participants exercise longer when working with a moderately superior virtual partner who provides no encouragement
coding_context.reported_success_quote:
Newly collected data corroborated Irwin et al.’s (2013) finding that encouragement using the
ambiguous and exclusive pronoun “you” (e.g. “you can do it”) from a virtually present partner
significantly weakened this Köhler effect. Some partial support was found for Irwin et al.’s expla-
nation of this effect. Irwin et al. suggested that when one hears one’s partner say things like “you
can do it!”, that may be interpreted that the partner is him/herself struggling and is to some degree
trying to encourage him/herself. Hence, that partner may not be as superior as previously thought.
